parsed_answer.content:
Virtual threads, introduced as part of Project Loom and standardized in Java 21, represent a paradigm shift in how we handle concurrent workloads on the Java Virtual Machine. Traditional platform threads map 1:1 to operating system threads, making them a scarce, expensive resource bound by kernel stack allocations (typically 1MB of memory) and expensive context switches. Virtual threads break this constraint by decoupling the application-level thread abstraction from the underlying OS thread, implementing an N:M scheduling model where millions of virtual threads (the N) are multiplexed across a much smaller pool of operating system threads known as carrier threads (the M). 

At the core of this runtime architecture is the concept of mounting and unmounting. A virtual thread does not own a dedicated carrier thread for its entire lifecycle. Instead, when a virtual thread is runnable and scheduled to execute, it is 'mounted' onto a carrier thread—meaning its stack chunk is associated with the carrier thread's stack, and execution proceeds on the CPU. Crucially, when a virtual thread encounters a blocking operation (such as I/O reads, waiting on a lock via java.util.concurrent.locks, or invoking Thread.sleep), it is 'unmounted'. The JVM intercepts the blocking action, detaches the virtual thread's stack chunk from the carrier thread, and saves its state. The carrier thread is then immediately freed to mount and execute another runnable virtual thread. Once the blocking condition resolves, the virtual thread becomes eligible for scheduling again and is mounted onto an available carrier thread, potentially a completely different OS thread than the one it started on.

rows: N:M mapping over a pool of carrier threads
Fixed, large stack size (~1MB initial allocation)
Dynamic, starts small (a few hundred bytes) and grows/shrinks
Expensive, involves OS system calls and kernel allocation
Extremely cheap, created purely in user-space memory
Blocks the underlying OS thread; idle CPU core waste
Unmounts from carrier thread; carrier executes other work

items: The underlying scheduler for virtual threads is a specialized ForkJoinPool operating in FIFO mode, configured by default to match the number of available processors (Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()).

Stack chunks for virtual threads are allocated on the JVM's garbage-collected heap as internal objects (implementation-specific structures), allowing them to grow and shrink dynamically as call depth fluctuates.

Monitors and synchronized blocks can 'pin' a virtual thread to its carrier thread. When a virtual thread executes inside a synchronized block or native method and performs a blocking operation, the JVM cannot unmount it because the carrier thread's stack holds native monitor ownership or native frames, forcing the OS thread to block alongside the virtual thread.
ReentrantLock and other java.util.concurrent synchronizers are fully virtual-thread-aware and will trigger an unmount safely without pinning the carrier thread.

parsed_answer.content: Beware of 'pinning' when migrating legacy codebases to virtual threads. If your application heavily relies on synchronized blocks, native methods, or JNI calls during blocking I/O, the virtual thread will pin its carrier thread, defeating the purpose of M:N scheduling and potentially starving the ForkJoinPool. Always refactor legacy blocking code to use java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock instead of synchronized keywords before adopting virtual thread pools.
